summary: The note is an overview of space weather and the September 2023 solar storm, which began with a flare from sunspot AR2867 and disrupted power grids, satellites, GPS, internet services and financial trading. It describes the cascade of impacts and the mitigation measures suggested for utilities, satellite operators, ISPs, financial institutions and individuals. It closes by stressing that improved forecasting by agencies like the SWPC will help with preparedness.
one_line: Overview of space weather and the September 2023 solar storm's impacts on power, satellites, internet and finance, plus mitigation and preparedness strategies.
key_facts: Space weather includes solar flares, sunspots, solar wind, and coronal mass ejections (CMEs), which send electromagnetic radiation and energized particles through space.
On September 10, 2023, a potent solar flare erupted from sunspot AR2867 and reached peak intensity within minutes.
Scientists at the Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) closely monitored the sunspot and predicted potential impacts on Earth.
On September 12, 2023, just under 48 hours after the flare, charged particles reached Earth and produced auroras visible in places like New York City and Paris.
Dr. Michelle Thomsen of the Planetary Science Institute warned of possible technological perturbations from the storm.

On September 13, 2023, parts of the North American power grid fluctuated due to geomagnetically induced currents (GICs); Northern Electrics reported outages affecting over a million customers across multiple states.
Satellite operators including GlobalSatCorp experienced service disruptions.
On September 14, 2023, a commercial flight en route to Chicago briefly lost its GPS signal, but backup systems kicked in.
Internet service provider WebFast faced service drops, and social media platforms saw a significant dip in traffic.
The New York Stock Exchange reported delays in transactions that were quickly resolved.
Utilities began upgrading infrastructure with better transformers and systems able to rapidly disconnect from the grid to prevent GIC damage.
Satellite mitigation includes radiation hardening, on-board anomaly detection and recovery software, and protocols for solar storm warnings, as discussed by Thomas Barton of GlobalSatCorp.
ISPs such as WebFast are reportedly considering multiple redundant data pathways, and financial institutions are urged to keep tested off-site backups and continuity plans.
Individuals can prepare by keeping battery packs charged, having alternative lighting, and stocking non-perishable food.
